meta.title: Who really said "At Last She Sleeps Alone"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Irvin Cobb is tied to this epitaph joke only late and loosely. The earliest dated version (1935) credits Will Rogers, and Benchley gets it by 1942.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'At Last She Sleeps Alone'?
meta.ogDescription: An epitaph joke credited to Cobb, Benchley and Will Rogers. The earliest dated version QI found (1935) names Rogers, and no work by Cobb contains it.

answer.label: Not proven to be Irvin Cobb — origin unknown
answer.authorDates: Earliest dated version found: 1935, credited to Will Rogers
answer.sourceLine: No work by Irvin Cobb is known to contain this line. Quote Investigator ↗ found it first in a 1935 book, credited to Will Rogers, and credited to Robert Benchley by 1942. Cobb’s name appears only later: in 1945 as admittedly unreliable rumor, and in an undated story in a 2001 encyclopedia. QI suggests the joke may have started anonymously.

source.heading: Where the line actually turns up

docMeta.dd: 1935 — Bawdy Ballads and Lusty Lyrics, p. 64, credited to Will Rogers (per Quote Investigator)
1942 — Thesaurus of Anecdotes, ed. Edmund Fuller, Anecdote 884, p. 153
1945 (Adams’s Woollcott biography, passed on as “not too reliable” rumor) and 2001 (The Encyclopedia of Louisville, undated)
Varies: “At last she sleeps alone,” “She sleeps alone at last,” “asleep—alone—at last”

source.excerpt: Will Rogers’ suggested epitaph for a much-married Hollywood matron: “At last she sleeps alone!”
trail: 1935: Bawdy Ballads and Lusty Lyrics gives the line as Will Rogers’ suggested epitaph for a much-married Hollywood matron. A longer party-game version, also credited to Rogers, appears in 1940 (Quote Investigator ↗).
1942: Thesaurus of Anecdotes tells a nearly identical party-game story with Robert Benchley writing the epitaph. Bennett Cerf repeats a Benchley version in 1944 (Quote Investigator ↗).

1945: Samuel Hopkins Adams’s biography of Alexander Woollcott lists “Irvin Cobb’s epitaph” for one “Polly Simpkins” among quips credited to the Algonquin crowd by “common, but not too reliable, rumor” (Quote Investigator ↗).
2001: In The Encyclopedia of Louisville, historian Thomas D. Clark writes that Cobb suggested “At Last She Sleeps Alone” for Sallie Ward, but gives no date (Quote Investigator ↗).
source.excerptNote: From Bawdy Ballads and Lusty Lyrics (1935), as transcribed by Quote Investigator. This is the earliest dated version QI found, and it credits Will Rogers, not Cobb. The Cobb story, about the much-married Louisville socialite Sallie Ward, comes from historian Thomas D. Clark writing in 2001, and Clark gives no date or source for it.

source.rightsNote: No author or original work for this wording can be identified. It circulated as an anonymous epitaph joke credited to several humorists, and none of Irvin Cobb’s known works contains it, so we claim no copyright status. The 1935 and later printed versions belong to the compilers who printed them, not to Cobb.

author.name: Irvin Cobb
author.heading: About Irvin Cobb
author.bio: Irvin S. Cobb was a humorist from Paducah, Kentucky. He moved to New York in 1904 and became the highest-paid staff reporter at Joseph Pulitzer’s New York World. He wrote more than 60 books and 300 short stories, including the Kentucky tales collected as Old Judge Priest (1915), and later acted in films and hosted the 1935 Academy Awards. His reputation as a Kentucky wit makes him a natural home for a joke about Louisville’s most-married belle.

copyAttribution: “At last she sleeps alone.” — origin unknown. The earliest dated version found (1935) credits Will Rogers; it was later credited to Robert Benchley (1942) and Irvin Cobb (1945, as rumor). Source: Quote Investigator, via Quotle.info.

misattribution.heading: Three humorists, one joke
misattribution.intro: This mock epitaph for a much-married woman has been credited to at least three famous wits. The anecdotes told about two of them are almost identical, which suggests the punch line came first and the famous names were added later.

items.why: Bartlett’s, the Oxford Dictionary of Humorous Quotations and the Yale Book of Quotations all credit Benchley. The earliest Benchley version QI found dates to 1942, after the 1935 Rogers version (Quote Investigator ↗).

The earliest Cobb credit QI found is from 1945. It uses different wording (“asleep—alone—at last”) and is passed on as “not too reliable” rumor. The Sallie Ward story is told without a date in a 2001 reference book (Quote Investigator ↗).

Credited in 1935 and again in 1940. QI says that on current evidence Rogers “deserves priority,” while noting that the story repeats almost word for word in the Benchley version (Quote Investigator ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody has shown that Irvin Cobb wrote or said this line. The earliest dated version found credits Will Rogers (1935), and Quote Investigator ↗ suggests the joke may have started anonymously before being pinned on well-known wits.

context.heading: A party-game punch line
lead: The joke is usually set at a Hollywood party where each guest writes their own epitaph. A much-married actress can’t think of anything, and the resident wit writes it for her. The 1940 Rogers version and the 1942 Benchley version tell this same scene almost word for word, which is the main reason Quote Investigator doubts either story as told.

Cobb’s version has a real person as its target: Sallie Ward of Louisville, who married four times. If Cobb did make the remark, QI notes he may have used the joke before the other two. No dated record of him saying it has been found, though.
context.pull: The near replication of the anecdote for Rogers and Benchley is suspicious.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI's earliest dated version is 1935, Bawdy Ballads and Lusty Lyrics p. 64, crediting Will Rogers ('much-married Hollywood matron'); 1940 Better Crops with Plant Food also credits Rogers

Earliest Benchley credit QI found is 1942, Thesaurus of Anecdotes (Anecdote 884, p. 153); Cerf, Try and Stop Me (1944), p. 133 gives 'She sleeps alone at last'; YBQ, Bartlett's and Oxford credit Benchley
1945 Adams biography of Woollcott credits 'Irvin Cobb's epitaph' for 'Polly Simpkins: asleep—alone—at last' as 'common, but not too reliable, rumor'
Thomas D. Clark, Encyclopedia of Louisville (2001), p. 921: Cobb suggested 'At Last She Sleeps Alone' for Sallie Ward; no date given; Sally Ward lived 1827–1896; Cobb 1876–1944

QI conclusion: at least three people linked; the near-identical Rogers/Benchley anecdotes are suspicious; Rogers deserves priority; the earliest Cobb credit comes after both; the joke may have started anonymously
Cobb: born June 23, 1876, Paducah; died March 11, 1944; moved to New York in 1904; New York World; Old Judge Priest (1915); 60+ books, 300 short stories; hosted the 7th Academy Awards (1935)
Sallie Ward (1827–1896), Louisville socialite, married four times
